transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-07 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya Patel, Ryan Chen (Redwood); Tom Keane, Priya Sharma, Marcus Lee (Galehound)

[00:00:02] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick intro from redwood side then jump into your latency and throughput goals.
[00:00:12] Tom: thanks Maya. quick note — we had a brief sync earlier, so Priya and Marcus are here to dig into perf details.
[00:00:20] Ryan: great, i'm ryan, i'm the se. i'll own the microbench and p95 tests. 
[00:00:28] Tom: quick context: Galehound is moving from a CPU-based in-house solution to a GPU-backed streaming pipeline. target is conversational assistants, short prompts ~30-80 tokens and longer completions up to 2k tokens. primary SLAs: 95th percentile latency under 200ms for short-turn responses and sustainable token/sec for sustained bursts.
[00:00:52] Priya: and we expect spikes — our front-end can fanout 1k concurrent users with ~2 requests/sec each during peak. so concurrency math matters.
[00:01:05] Maya: ok that's helpful. curious — are you more focused on single-request p95 or end-to-end UX p95 including frontend and networking?
[00:01:14] Tom: the former, server-side p95 is the gating number. we can tune frontend separately.
[00:01:20] Marcus: Also want to confirm data flows — we're allowed to send prompts to hosted services as long as PII is removed. For PHI or regulated flows we'll need Private with VPC and KMS.
[00:01:33] Ryan: makes sense. quick to the benchmarking plan: we'll measure p95 under 5 concurrency scenarios: 1, 8, 64, 256, 1024. streaming enabled for the chat path, and we'll capture tokens/sec and end-to-end server p95.
[00:01:52] Priya: when you say streaming enabled, do you mean chunked response streaming or true server side incremental tokens? we care about reconnects/resume.
[00:02:03] Ryan: yes chunked streaming, like SSE/WebSocket streaming. Redwood's streaming path keeps KV cache between calls if pinned, and we can simulate reconnect behavior.
[00:02:15] Tom: good. a few tradeoffs we worry about: Hosted is easiest but worried about noisy neighbors and unpredictable p95 during token storms. Dedicated solves that but costs more. Private is our preferred for regulated customers but ops overhead increases.
[00:02:30] Maya: that's the classic tradeoff. we usually recommend Hosted for pilots where data residency isn't required, Dedicated for predictable p95 and throughput, and Private for strict compliance. but there are tactical options — Dedicated with VPC peering is possible.
[00:02:44] Marcus: peering latency — what's typical? if our app sits in GCP us-central and Dedicated is in AWS us-west-2 that adds unpredictability.
[00:02:53] Ryan: yep, network hop matters. in our experience <5ms intra-region peering, cross-region can be 20-50ms. we recommend aligning region with your app.
[00:03:03] Priya: ok can we talk numbers: for a 3B quantized model, what throughput can we expect per GPU for streaming?
[00:03:11] Ryan: rough ballpark: with continuous batching disabled, streaming overhead lowers throughput relative to pure batch. for a 3B quant model on an A100 class node we often see 800-1500 tokens/sec single-stream baseline; with optimized kernels and prefix KV cache, sustained aggregate can be 4k-6k tokens/sec per GPU depending on sequence length distribution.
[00:03:35] Tom: that aligns with some vendor numbers we've seen, though ModelHoster advertised higher numbers but with caveats.
[00:03:43] Maya: can i ask about p95 numbers under multiplexed streaming?
[00:03:48] Ryan: sure — p95 depends heavily on queueing and batching. with continuous batching and SLO for 200ms p95 on short responses, you'd want reserved Dedicated slices sized to keep queue depth low. we can hit sub-200ms p95 for 16-32 concurrent streams per GPU for short 40-token responses. when you scale to 256-1024 concurrent streams, you'll need multiple GPUs and routing to maintain p95.
[00:04:15] Priya: what's the impact of KV-cache hits?
[00:04:20] Ryan: KV-cache hits reduce decoder compute — if you can cache prefixes across the conversation, p95 improves significantly, often cutting p95 by 20-40% for repeated context patterns. there's complexity in cache warmup on cold starts which we'll test.
[00:04:36] Marcus: what about tokenization variance? sometimes our prompts expand to 1.5x tokens in model space which changes token/sec math.
[00:04:44] Ryan: yes account for tokenizer overhead; we'll include token inflation tests in the microbench.
[00:04:50] Tom: security question — for Dedicated can we have customer-managed KMS and audit logs?
[00:04:56] Maya: yes, Dedicated supports KMS integration and audit logs; Private adds more controls like air-gapped and HSM if needed.
[00:05:04] Priya: any documented SLOs for streaming p95? we saw a doc but it was general.
[00:05:10] Maya: i'll send the streaming SLO doc, it has measured p50/p95/p99 for a bunch of model families, plus our Recommended Batch sizes. link: https://redwood.example/docs/streaming-slos (note: placeholder).
[00:05:22] Tom: perfect. can you walk through an example test scenario so our infra team can map it?
[00:05:27] Ryan: sure. test plan sketch: 1) baseline single-stream latency with warm KV-cache; 2) ramp to concurrency target following your real-world curve (we'll use the 1k concurrent users example); 3) run sustained token/sec for 5-10 minutes to detect thermal or GC effects; 4) inject reconnects and partial messages to validate resume and caching behavior; 5) measure p95/p99 and tokens/sec across phases.
[00:05:57] Marcus: for step 2 how do you route traffic? sticky sessions?
[00:06:01] Ryan: Redwood can route by session affinity to keep KV-cache local to the worker pool; for high availability we have automatic routing fallback to other pools but that invalidates cache. we'll test both sticky and stateless routing.
[00:06:14] Priya: about quantization — we use 4-bit in prod experiments. does Redwood support int4 inference and how does that affect p95?
[00:06:22] Ryan: yes we support quantized execution paths. int4 reduces memory and can increase throughput but kernel-level inaccuracies can cause mild quality regressions. performance-wise you often gain 1.5-2x tokens/sec; we'll include a quality/regression check in the pilot.
[00:06:37] Tom: and what about warmup patterns for cold starts? if a pod restarts, how long to warm KV-cache and cold pipeline?
[00:06:45] Ryan: cold start is primarily model load time + cache rebuild. with warm model pinned on Dedicated, model load time is amortized; typical cold start for large models can be 10-30s if model isn't preloaded. we recommend preloading pools for strict SLOs.
[00:06:58] Maya: ok let's lock some acceptance criteria you mentioned: server-side p95 <200ms for short-turns at 16-32 concurrent streams per GPU, aggregate tokens/sec 4k sustained per GPU, and predictable p95 behavior under 5-minute sustained bursts. any additions?
[00:07:16] Priya: add cache-warmup time and reconnection handling must be <=2x normal latency.
[00:07:21] Tom: also audit log retention of 90 days for compliance.
[00:07:26] Maya: noted.
[00:07:28] [00:07:30] Speaker 2 (transcription noise): um -- sorry background noise --
[00:07:34] Marcus: slight crosstalk, sorry.
[00:07:37] Ryan: no worries. jumping to pricing: Dedicated reserved pools come with commit tiers and burst capacity. Maya can share the sheet after.
[00:07:46] Maya: yes i'll share tiers. Pilot usually runs on a small Dedicated pool, we do the tests, then propose a commit to match sustained needs.
[00:07:55] Tom: about fallback policies — if a Dedicated pool is saturated during an unexpected surge can you fall back to Hosted cheaper variants automatically?
[00:08:04] Ryan: yes we support smart routing and fallbacks by policy — you can define graceful degradation to a smaller model variant or to Hosted, with weighted routing. we can test failover scenarios too.
[00:08:16] Priya: do you have instrumentation we can push to our tracing? can we correlate trace IDs?
[00:08:21] Maya: Redwood Console exposes per-request IDs and supports tracing hooks; we can provide a small tracing adapter to forward spans.
[00:08:29] Tom: great. on legal/compliance: can you share a sample DPA and SOC2 cert?
[00:08:33] Maya: yes, i'll attach SOC2 report and DPA in the follow-up.
[00:08:38] Ryan: last technical nit: for reconnects we emulate partial-chunk lost and reconnection behavior; some vendors mishandle seq numbers which causes duplicate tokens. we'll validate correctness as part of tests.
[00:08:52] Priya: any gotchas for caching when users multi-device? session affinity could be problematic.
[00:08:58] Ryan: for multi-device you either centralize cache or rebuild context per device; there's tradeoff between memory and latency. we'll test a multi-device workflow in the pilot.
[00:09:09] Tom: ok, what's the minimal pilot to prove this?
[00:09:12] Maya: a 2-week pilot: provision 2-4 Dedicated GPUs with your model, run the microbench and streaming scenarios, provide logs and Console access, and review quality/regression. if successful, move to commit.
[00:09:25] Marcus: timeline wise we want results in 2 weeks.
[00:09:28] Maya: we'll aim for a May 18 pilot kickoff as mentioned. Ryan will run preflight microbench next week.
[00:09:36] Ryan: i'll need prompt set and expected concurrency curve.
[00:09:40] Tom: we'll send those by May 12.
[00:09:44] [00:09:46] Speaker 3: um.. small audio glitch earlier, sorry if we missed anything.
[00:09:49] Maya: no problem. quick recap: deliverables — Ryan runs microbench and shares results; Maya shares pricing, SOC2, and streaming SLO doc; Galehound provides prompts and traffic curve. Pilot kickoff May 18.
[00:10:04] Tom: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[00:10:08] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.

Note: Transcription includes occasional speaker mislabels and filler words; some technical terms may be slightly garbled (e.g., KV-cache sometimes transcribed as "K V cache").
